newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Beleaguered Bulgarian Socialists call for more talks.
newsitem.headline: Beleaguered Bulgarian Socialists call for more talks.

text.p: Bulgaria's beleaguered Socialist rulers invited their opponents for talks on Monday but warned that if they failed they would present a new Socialist cabinet to parliament on Tuesday.
With time running out for formation of a cabinet, and the party split on whether to put a team together or hand back the mandate, party leaders ended six hours of talks with a new call for dialogue.

Student demonstrators surrounded the party headquarters chanting anti-communist slogans and brandishing effigies of party leader Georgi Parvanov and Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, the party's nominee for premier.
Protesters backing opposition demands for an immediate general election staged a 28th day of strikes, rallies and blockades around the country.

The Socialists proposed negotiations with the mediation of President Petar Stoyanov on formation of a new cabinet. The opposition held one round of talks with the Socialists then refused to meet them again.
"If there is no agreement with the political forces, parliament will vote on the cabinet proposed by the Democratic Left," said a party statement.
It said the Socialists were prepared to discuss a cabinet with the mandate of other parliamentary groups, but Parvanov said he expected his majority party to be represented.

The cabinet should prepare a new state budget, legal measures for introduction of a fixed exchange rate regime and other steps to tackle the economic crisis, and should hold negotiations with the International Monetary Fund, the statement said.
Parvanov said that once the crisis was stabilised, the cabinet could transform itself into an interim, caretaker administration at the end of April and organise elections in June.

Bulgaria, edging towards economic collapse, urgently needs a credible government to negotiate with foreign lenders and set up a tough fixed exchange rate regime to restore confidence in the national currency.

If the Socialists do form a cabinet and present it to parliament for approval, many people fear a repeat of the violence which broke out between police and demonstrators who besieged and ransacked parliament on January 10.
Dobrev tried on Friday to propose a compromise way out but failed to win the backing of the party leadership.
"The BSP has two choices, either to go in peace or to go in war, and we are prepared for both," opposition leader Ivan Kostov told the daily rally in Sofia.
At Doupnitsa, 60 km (35 miles) south of Sofia, several hundred opposition supporters blocked road and rail links to Greece for a fifth day.
Protesters warmed themselves at wood fires on barricades and said that if the Socialists formed a new cabinet they would set up their barricades outside parliament.
Miners and steelworkers went on strike, and protesters blocked main roads around the second city of Plovdiv and the highway to the border with the former Yugoslav republic of Macedonia.
State radio said distribution staff at the Neftohim refinery were operating only a minimum service, supplying schools, hospitals and the police.
In Sofia, students blocked road junctions and calmly set up chessboards or played cards on tram lines.
Thousands of opposition supporters, workers and students, blaming the Socialists for economic collapse, have staged daily anti-government rallies since January 6 to demand elections.
They accuse the Socialists and their powerful business allies of carrying out only superficial reforms while siphoning public money abroad.
